title: Rehearsal in PD
author: Peps Mccrea
summary: Peps Mccrea closes out a professional-development-themed run of his Evidence Snacks newsletter with a compact case for rehearsal - practising a teaching change outside the classroom, alone or with a coach - as one of the two most essential ingredients of effective PD alongside modelling. His argument rests on cognitive capacity: making any change to teaching requires coordinating unfamiliar combinations of thought, speech, and posture simultaneously, and the classroom itself is already too demanding an environment to absorb that extra load while also managing students, so practice needs to happen somewhere distraction-free and emotionally safe first. He offers three techniques for maximizing rehearsal's impact: shrinking the change to one small modification at a time rather than several at once, running multiple rehearsal rounds with feedback between each from a peer, coach, or self-review video, and gradually increasing the authenticity of the practice conditions as mastery builds. Mccrea is candid that rehearsal feels uncomfortable at first, since it requires focusing on oneself and opening up to visible failure in front of colleagues, which is precisely why teachers default to more comfortable but less powerful PD activities like discussion and reflection. He closes by pointing readers to a working paper by Mancenido et al. on rehearsal and responsive teaching for those wanting the underlying evidence base.
points: Mccrea's core argument is capacity-based: teaching requires coordinating "novel sequences of thought, speech, posture" in real time inside an already cognitively demanding classroom, leaving little spare bandwidth to also practice a brand-new change live.

His three technique refinements - shrink the change, run multiple rounds with feedback, ramp up authenticity - form a deliberate progression from safe, distraction-free rehearsal toward classroom-realistic conditions.

He explicitly ranks rehearsal above discussion and reflection as PD activities, arguing the latter feel more comfortable precisely because they avoid the self-focused vulnerability that makes rehearsal actually effective.
The closing pointer to Mancenido et al.'s working paper on rehearsal and responsive teaching signals the piece is summarizing an evidence base rather than offering personal opinion alone.
quotes: Rehearsal is when we practise a change to our teaching outside the classroom, either on our own or (even better) with the support of a colleague or coach.

Making a change to our teaching requires the repeated co-ordination of novel sequences of thought, speech, posture, and more—all at once. The classroom is already a highly cognitively demanding environment.
It's best to focus on one small change at a time, rather than trying to implement multiple modifications and not doing any of them well enough to count (or last).

The best rehearsal entails planning what we will do when we get to the classroom, and then rehearsing this several times while getting feedback between each round (from a peer, coach, or yourself using video).
To butcher a phrase from Big Dawg Lemov... "don't practise till you get it right [outside the classroom], practise till you can't get it wrong [inside the classroom].
